The appeal was made on Saturday by the Madaki of Kpaduma 2 and secretary-general of the community, Simon Baba-Yerima, who said affected residents had remained stranded for several months due to the absence of road infrastructure in the new settlement.
Baba-Yerima, who spoke on behalf of the community during a press briefing, commended Wike for completing the road project earlier this year and approving an alternative settlement within the community’s ancestral territory for those whose properties were affected.
He explained that the community cooperated with the project after reaching an understanding with the FCT administration that residents would not be displaced from their ancestral land or relocated to unfamiliar communities.
“We are proud of the minister and appreciate what he has done. We cooperated with the development because we welcomed it as a host community. That was why the project commenced peacefully and was also executed without any problem,” he said.
According to him, the affected residents willingly removed their structures within the road corridor following engagements with the minister and the subsequent approval of land for their resettlement within the Kpaduma domain.
He disclosed that the community identified an undeveloped portion of its land for the relocation exercise, which received the minister’s approval, adding that beneficiaries had been issued allocation documents and Certificates of Occupancy (C-of-O), in addition to monetary compensation.
However, he lamented that the absence of access roads had prevented the beneficiaries from moving to their new plots, leaving many families to depend on relatives for accommodation.
“The challenge we are facing now is the issue of road connectivity. The road construction in the new layout has not been done. Our people would have moved there, completed their houses and settled down, but there is no access.
“For several months now, they have continued to squat with family members, which is not a habitable situation. Some people had their houses demolished and were expected to relocate, but they cannot do so because they cannot access the new settlement,” he said.
The community leader described the situation as increasingly distressing, noting that the affected families had been waiting for the completion of the resettlement process despite receiving the necessary allocation documents.
He appealed to Wike to treat the construction of the access roads as an urgent intervention, stressing that the provision of land and compensation would not amount to meaningful resettlement until the beneficiaries could move into their permanent homes.
Baba-Yerima further explained that the community’s position was rooted in its longstanding demand for recognition, integration and protection of the rights of indigenous communities within the FCT.
He recalled that Kpaduma community had pursued legal action over its fundamental rights, particularly its demand to remain on its ancestral land and be integrated into the development of the nation’s capital.
“We have been in court seeking justice because this is our ancestral home. We believe we have the right to remain here and be integrated into the urban development of the Federal Capital Territory.
“The approval given by the minister for our people to be resettled within our domain is a demonstration of that integration, and we appreciate the political will he has shown,” he stated.
He clarified that the resettlement arrangement was specifically for families whose properties were affected by the road construction and did not constitute a comprehensive relocation programme for the entire Kpaduma community.
He also acknowledged the role of the FCT Department of Resettlement and Compensation in conducting demographic surveys, assessments and evaluations of indigenous communities to establish their circumstances and possible resettlement needs.
While expressing confidence in the minister’s commitment to infrastructure delivery, Baba-Yerima urged him to ensure that the Kuruduma layout was not left without the basic facilities required for habitation.
He cited Wike’s public commitment to completing projects within specified timelines, saying the minister should extend the same determination to the resettlement arrangement.
“I have heard the minister say several times that he does not start a project and abandon it halfway. He gives timelines and ensures that projects are completed.
“We are grateful for the projects he has executed and the ones he has commissioned. This particular one should also receive attention so that our people can move into their new homes,” he said.
The Kpaduma community leader expressed optimism that the access roads could be completed within one month if the minister gave the project the required attention.
“My appeal to the Honourable Minister is that he should complete the work he has started for us. The layout he approved for our people at Paduma needs access roads so that we can begin construction and move into our houses.
“I know he can do it, even within one month. I believe that once this appeal gets to him, he will take immediate action,” Baba-Yerima added.
He reiterated the community’s appreciation for the minister’s intervention but insisted that the construction of the road network remained essential to bringing the resettlement process to completion and ending the accommodation difficulties confronting affected families.
